data.title: 56,197 Americans Now at Risk of Fraud – Names, Social Security Numbers, Financial Records and More Potentially Exposed
data.description:
A Wyoming orthopedic practice has disclosed a cyberattack that put the personal, financial and medical records of tens of thousands of people at risk.

The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services says Casper Orthopedic Associates PC suffered a hacking/IT incident on July 23rd, impacting 56,197 people.

In a notice to impacted individuals, the healthcare firm says an unauthorized entity accessed its systems and stole files that may include patients’ first names, last names, dates of birth, driver’s license numbers, Social Security numbers, financial account records, and medical information.

“On or about May 23, 2026, Casper discovered it was the victim of a cyberattack by an unauthorized third party. Immediately upon identifying the incident, Casper engaged third-party cybersecurity experts to assess, contain, and remediate the incident. Law enforcement was also notified.

Casper’s investigation, which concluded on June 11, 2026, determined that the unauthorized party may have acquired sensitive information from Casper’s systems. Casper then undertook an in-depth review process of the impacted information to determine the impacted individuals and their address information, which was completed on September 2, 2026. As such, Casper notified those who are believed to be impacted on September 8, 2026.”

Casper says it has found no evidence that anyone’s information was specifically misused.

The practice has added safeguards and tightened physical security while urging affected patients to reach out to credit reporting agencies such as Equifax, Experian and TransUnion.

Casper Orthopedic Associates PC is an orthopedic practice based in Casper, Wyoming.

data.title: New Hampshire Bank ATM Loader Accused of Stealing $259,574, Spending the Loot on Cars, Luxury Cruise
data.description:
An armored truck driver hired to load cash into ATMs has been accused of stealing $259,574 from the machines and spending the money on cars, a cruise and other purchases.

Federal prosecutors say Christopher Skinner, 41, formerly of Milford, New Hampshire, worked alone at ATM locations across the state and removed cash bundles before servicing the machines between February 2nd and February 26th of 2024.

A federal indictment charges Skinner with 18 counts of bank theft plus money laundering and conspiracy counts tied to two FDIC-insured banks. His partner, Amee Skinner, 37, formerly of Conway, faces related laundering counts. Both pleaded not guilty in U.S. District Court for the District of New Hampshire and are presumed innocent.

Prosecutors say cash deposits into the couple’s accounts rose sharply afterward, and funded the purchase of cars, a luxury cruise and other purchases.

“The defendants allegedly used the stolen funds to make substantial personal purchases, including $40,000 in cash for a 2019 GMC Sierra and $28,814 in cash for a 2019 Lincoln Nautilus. According to the indictment, the defendants also used stolen funds to pay for additional travel, retail, and online purchases.”

If convicted, the Skinners face years in prison.

“The bank theft counts each carry a maximum prison term of 10 years. The money laundering counts carry a maximum prison term of 10 years, and the money laundering conspiracy count carries a maximum term of 20 years.”

The indictment was filed August 5th of 2026.

data.title: $80,000,000+ in JPMorgan Chase and Wells Fargo Belonging to Montana Payments Firm Abruptly Seized Over Potential Fraud
data.description:
U.S. prosecutors have seized nearly $84 million from bank accounts and cryptocurrency wallets tied to a Montana payments firm linked to Tether.

The civil forfeiture targets Capstone, a money services business that allegedly posed as an information technology company to open accounts at major banks while moving money for crypto firms, reports Reuters.

Court filings say Capstone, registered in Montana, processed payments for two crypto companies through a bank in Dominica. Prosecutors say the firm also ran a scheme that converted fraud proceeds into crypto by posing as FBI agents.

Nearly $81 million was seized from Capstone accounts at Wells Fargo and about $2 million from an account at JPMorgan Chase. Roughly $1.2 million worth of Tether’s dollar-pegged token was taken as well, according to the July filing first reported by The Information.

Tether said it was a customer of the Dominica bank and that its assets there were limited. A spokesperson addressed Capstone’s alleged conduct.

“Tether had no knowledge of the conduct by Capstone alleged by the Department of Justice.”

The Justice Department did not allege wrongdoing by Tether or the other firms involved. Spokespeople for Wells Fargo and JPMorgan declined to comment.

A lawyer for Capstone told Reuters the firm denies wrongdoing and plans to challenge the complaint.

Tether issues USDT, a dollar-pegged cryptocurrency used to move value on crypto networks.

data.title: Banks Risk Losing $230,000,000,000 in Payments Revenue As Stablecoins and Tokenized Deposits Scale, According to Survey
data.description:
Banks risk losing $230 billion in payments revenue as stablecoins, tokenized deposits and central bank digital currencies move into wider use, according to a survey conducted by IT services and consulting firm Capgemini.

Capgemini’s World Payments Report 2027 projects those instruments will make up about 4% of global payments volume by 2030, pressuring foreign exchange spreads, correspondent banking, float income and transaction fees that banks thrive on, says Capgemini.

The study says about $4 trillion sits trapped in accounts used to fund cross-border settlement. Nearly 60% of large corporates would take stablecoin services from non-banks if their banks fall behind, even though 71% still prefer banks for tokenized payments when cost and quality are equal.

Only 21% of banks are actively scaling at least one of these tools. Tokenized deposits ranked as banks’ top near-term priority because they stay on balance sheets and fit existing rules. Leaders that are already scaling are three times more likely to find new revenue streams and expect to offset losses in 15 months versus 25 months for other banks.

Capgemini’s global head of payment services Jeroen Hölscher framed the stakes for lenders.

“With $230 billion at stake, banks must decide what role they want to play in this emerging ecosystem.”

The report surveyed 1,110 corporates with more than $1 billion in revenue and 300 banking executives across nine markets. Capgemini is a global consulting and technology firm headquartered in Paris, France.

data.title: Major US City Launching $8,000,000 No-Strings-Attached Guaranteed Income Program That Pays Enrollees Hundreds of Dollars Monthly
data.description:
The City of Sacramento is launching an $8 million guaranteed income program that will pay eligible foster youth $900 a month with no strings attached.

The city and United Way California Capital Region say the Foster Youth Guaranteed Income Program will send the money for up to two years, or until a recipient turns 25, whichever comes first.

Applications open October 1st of 2026 and close at 11:59 p.m. on October 31st of 2026. One hundred eligible applicants will be chosen by lottery, with notices starting the first week of November. Payments are set to begin January 15th of 2027.

Applicants must be ages 16 to 23 when payments start, live in the city or county of Sacramento, or be receiving homeless services there. They must be former foster youth who left care after age 16, or current foster youth within 90 days of leaving when payments start. Household income has to sit at or below 300% of the federal poverty level. Immigration status does not affect eligibility.

Recipients do not have to join any other services to keep the checks. They can spend the money as they choose.

The city is paying for the program with Measure L, the 2022 Sacramento Children’s Fund that requires the equivalent of 40% of local cannabis tax revenue to go to child and youth services.

United Way California Capital Region will run the program. The nonprofit has administered guaranteed-income pilots in the region since 2021.

Mayor Kevin McCarty addressed the funding.

“Supporting former foster youth as they transition into adulthood is an investment in their future and our community’s future. We’re putting our Measure L funding where it can have the greatest impact.”

data.title: Minneapolis Bank Teller Allegedly Steals Nearly $41,000, Covers Up by Fabricating Records and Swapping Real Cash With Fake Bills
data.description:
A Minneapolis bank teller is accused of stealing nearly $41,000 by falsifying records and swapping real cash for counterfeit bills before disappearing from the job, and possibly heading to the Bahamas.

Kendrell Lashawna Maliya Stuart, 25, faces a felony theft-by-swindle charge tied to the U.S. Bank branch at 4930 34th Avenue South in Minneapolis, reports FOX 9. The charge carries up to 20 years in prison and a $100,000 fine.

A U.S. Bank investigator told the court Stuart allegedly falsified teller records and stole about $40,999 in cash from the branch where she worked.

The shortages surfaced in stages. On May 30th of 2026, the branch cash vault was short $32,000. On June 1st, another $1,000 went missing from the vault. On June 5th, Stuart reported her own assigned cash box was short $1,999.94. She then stopped reporting for work and asked for a leave of absence.

On June 9th, a cash audit found $6,000 in counterfeit bills, described as motion picture money, stored with mutilated currency in the vault, leaving the vault another $6,000 short, the complaint states. Bank records and video surveillance allegedly showed Stuart entering cash transfers from her cash box to the vault without placing the physical cash inside.

As of July 29th of 2026, she had not returned to work and U.S. Bank terminated her for theft, according to the complaint. Minneapolis police’s Financial Crimes Unit received a report of the theft on August 19th.

Hennepin County District Court Judge Jamie L. Anderson issued a warrant for Stuart’s arrest, with bail set at $100,000. She is not in custody. The complaint states social media indicates she could be in the Bahamas, her native home.

U.S. Bank is a major American bank with branches nationwide.

data.title: Massachusetts Woman Steals $536,000 From Bank Accounts Using Fake Driver’s Licenses: DOJ
data.description:
A Massachusetts woman is heading to federal prison after pulling $536,000 from bank accounts with fake driver’s licenses.

Rosemary Parks, 59, of Hopkinton, was sentenced on September 30th to 26 months, two years of supervised release and $4,000 in restitution, says the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Massachusetts.

Parks pleaded guilty in May to bank fraud and aggravated identity theft. She was arrested in January of 2026.

Between August and October of 2024, she impersonated at least eight customers at banks in Massachusetts and Rhode Island.

She used fake driver’s licenses that carried the customers’ information with her own photo, and handed tellers withdrawal slips with their names and account numbers.

She took the money in cashier’s checks and one cash withdrawal.

The case is tied to a wider investigation.

In July of 2025, six men were charged in a related multi-million-dollar scheme aimed at banks in Massachusetts, Connecticut and Rhode Island.

Phalentz Vernot, Victor Kolawole and Keith Wainaina have pleaded guilty and are awaiting sentencing.

Co-defendant William Shaw also pleaded guilty on September 30th in a related scheme.

He is set to be sentenced on January 6th, 2027.

data.title: Department of Justice Says UCLA Law Discriminated Against White and Asian Applicants
data.description:
The Justice Department says UCLA’s law school discriminated against white and Asian applicants in its 2023, 2024 and 2025 classes.

The findings say the school violated Title VI of the Civil Rights Act and the Supreme Court’s 2023 ban on race in admissions.

The department says the school rejected white and Asian applicants who had the same LSAT scores as admitted black and Hispanic applicants.

In 2024 and 2025 combined, half of the admitted black applicants had LSAT scores at or below 90 percent of the admitted white applicants.

Investigators say the application still uses essays that draw out race, and staff told applicants how to reveal it at a “Diversity Admissions Open House.”

Says Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon,

“Like many of its peer institutions, UCLA Law School runs a two-tiered admissions system whose academic bar for acceptance shifts up or down depending on the color of your skin.

The use of race as a thumb on the scale that helps or disadvantages any student is illegal. The Department will continue to enforce equal treatment under the law everywhere — including in our nation’s law schools.”

UCLA Law is the law school at the University of California, Los Angeles. It takes federal money, which puts it under the civil rights rule.

The department says it will try to settle. If that fails, it will sue.

data.title: Florida Man Masterminds Nationwide $3,010,000 Staffing and Payroll Fraud Scheme, Sentenced to 12 Years in Prison
data.description:
A Florida man has been sentenced to 12 years in federal prison and ordered to pay $3.01 million after admitting he led a scheme that defrauded staffing and payroll companies.

Crispian Atkins, 52, of Valrico, pleaded guilty on May 20th to conspiracy to commit wire fraud, wire fraud and aggravated identity theft, says the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Middle District of Florida.

U.S. District Judge Virginia M. Hernandez Covington sentenced him on September 29th of, 2026.

Court papers show the scheme ran from May of 2021 through March of 2024 and hit 10 companies that provide employment, payroll and financing services. The victim companies are located across the US.

Atkins and others falsely claimed they had landed information technology contracts and needed staffing or financing to do the work.

Some firms hired the group as temporary employees so they could complete the purported work.

Atkins then sent in fake timesheets so the companies would wire pay for work that was not real.

Prosecutors say the group moved the money through other accounts, took out cash to hide the source and split the proceeds.

In addition to the prison term, the court ordered Atkins to pay $3.01 million in restitution and forfeit the proceeds of the criminal conduct to the tune of $1.56 million.

The FBI’s Tampa Division and its Reno office investigated, with help from the Norwood Police Department in Massachusetts and the Polk County Sheriff’s Office.

data.title: Dual U.S.-Peruvian National Accused of Orchestrating at Least $40,000,000 in Fraudulent Bank Loans Extradited to Houston
data.description:
A 70-year-old dual U.S.-Peruvian citizen has been brought back to Houston to face charges in a bank fraud scheme that allegedly took in at least $40 million in loan proceeds.

The IRS Criminal Investigation says Hugo Villanueva, formerly of Katy, Texas, made his first appearance in Houston federal court after extradition from Peru on September 17th, 2026.

Prosecutors allege that from at least 2016 to 2021, Villanueva and others filed dozens of loan applications with false information and forged documents, including equipment invoices, tax returns and bank statements.

Villanueva himself is also accused of preparing false tax returns and financial statements to get the fraudulent loans approved.

He left the United States in 2023 before his arrest in Lima, Peru, in November of 2025.

Co-defendant Bun Khath, 45, of Richmond, has pleaded guilty and received a 120-month sentence. Meanwhile, co-defendants Jeremiah Almaguer and Jennifer Williams received 60 months and 12 months, respectively. Three other defendants have pleaded guilty and are awaiting sentencing.

Villanueva faces a detention hearing on October 7th.

“Villanueva faces up to 30 years in prison and a possible $1 million maximum fine for the conspiracy, bank fraud, and false statement to obtain credit charges. He also faces up to 20 years in prison and a possible $500,000 maximum fine or twice the amount of the value involved in the transaction for the money laundering conspiracy charge.”
